sm: The hosts, John Bickley and Georgia Howe, open the Thursday evening show with the day's top stories. Six people are dead in Washington after a man ended a shooting spree by taking his own life. It began around 8 a.m. in the Logan Circle neighborhood, about a mile from the White House, where he shot a person at a gym and then killed four more before locking himself in a seventh floor apartment. Officials say he shot himself while on the phone with police negotiators, and at least one more gym victim is in critical condition. Mayor Muriel Bowser thanked police, fire and EMS for containing the lone gunman.

Search crews are digging through rubble in New York City after a three-story building unexpectedly collapsed on Wednesday near Bedford and Flatbush in Brooklyn. An entire side of the apartment complex fell into a hole made by a construction crew working next door, leaving apartments exposed to the sidewalk. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at least eight people were killed, including two children, and at least eighteen were injured. Officials are unsure how many people were inside, so the numbers could rise. The mayor praised first responders and construction workers who dug victims out of the rubble.

Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO and president of Nvidia, the company he founded over three decades ago, amid fallout from an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. He also reportedly had a separate affair, revealed yesterday, with Nvidia's vice president of health care. Nvidia, worth an estimated four trillion dollars, makes the chips powering artificial intelligence. CFO Colette Kress will serve as CEO until a replacement is found. Separately, California Democrat Ro Khanna, a loud advocate for banning congressional stock trading, faces scrutiny for selling a large portion of his Nvidia stock hours before the scandal became public. He says his in-laws manage his investments in an independent trust, which logged more than 5,400 trades last year.

A migrant caravan of roughly 2,000 people is moving north through Mexico, hoping last week's Democratic midterm victories will improve their chances of entering the United States. One Nicaraguan migrant said Democrats will not let the Latino vote be lost. Border czar Tom Homan warned that caravans can come to the border all they want but will not be released into the country. He said authorities will turn them around or prosecute them, as the Trump administration maintains its hardline border policies.

President Trump is pulling Vice President Vance out of efforts to negotiate an end to the war with Iran and directing him instead to investigate alleged fraud in Democratic-run cities and states. Trump said we don't need a deal with Iran, despite the ongoing standoff over the Strait of Hormuz. Vance had recently contacted Iranian officials through Qatari mediators to propose renewed talks. Meanwhile, Pete Hegseth and staffers drew a reprimand at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier after being heard laughing following a photo op. A sentinel, Specialist Thomas Iglesias, demanded silence and respect. The Pentagon said he correctly reminded everyone to maintain decorum, and Hegseth praised him on X.

Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola lost a motion in court as ballots continue to be counted in Alaska, the final midterm Senate race yet to be called. With 86 percent reported, she leads by just under 4,000 votes. She asked for a report on why certain mail-in ballots were rejected, but Judge Thomas Matthews called the request not reasonable. Both major candidates will likely stay under 50 percent, triggering ranked choice voting. After the final count, likely in about a week, third-party ballots will be reassigned to Peltola or Sullivan based on second choices.

Conservative commentator Scott Jennings is asking a federal court to dismiss a 72.5 million dollar defamation lawsuit filed by streamer Hassan Piker. Piker sued over comments on Jennings's radio show accusing him of calling for black voters to be lynched, based on a video clip shared by the National Republican Senatorial Committee. Piker says the clip removed context showing he was sarcastically quoting another commentator. Jennings's attorney argues the video accurately captures Piker's words and that interpreting intended meaning cannot support defamation. The motion adds that Piker, a public figure, cannot show actual malice. Piker seeks 27.5 million in compensatory and 45 million in punitive damages.

Greta Thunberg sparked online backlash after laughing when she learned that the Fridays for Future movement she founded in 2018 was still holding demonstrations. In an interview for a new documentary, she was told the group was protesting in Berlin that day, then burst into laughter and said, really, they still do that. The 23-year-old has shifted much of her activism toward Gaza, including a flotilla to deliver aid. Critics online mocked her reaction. The hosts then recapped earlier stories, including Democrats promising to bring back deported migrants and an investigation into Gavin Newsom's wine empire, and said the show returns tomorrow morning.
sg: Jennings seeks dismissal of Piker suit
